description: examples/fullstack/main.go hardcodes SecretKey "replace-with-a-32-byte-minimum-secret-in-production!" (52 bytes, passes the 32-byte MinSecretKeyLength gate) and docs/content/docs/sdk/tokens-and-http.md publishes SecretKey "super-secret-32-byte-key-here!!!" (exactly 32 bytes, passes the gate). Both strings are public on GitHub, so any deployment that copy-pastes the example/docs without replacing the key mints HS256 tokens with an attacker-known key: the attacker replays the published string into their own jwt.New instance and forges access tokens the victim verifies. PoC test proves cross-instance forgery for both literals. Mitigating context: both sites carry replace-me comments and the library itself panics on short keys (TASK-067) — the gap is that a syntactically valid, publicly-known key is indistinguishable from a real one at construction.
remediation: Replace both literals with a crypto/rand generation snippet (e.g. `key := make([]byte, 32); rand.Read(key)` plus hex/base64 encode) and a warning that the value must come from a secret manager; never publish a valid-length key. Consider adding a denylist in jwt.New/Validate rejecting these exact published strings so copy-paste deployments fail fast. Docs example should use an obviously-invalid placeholder (e.g. <32 bytes) or os.Getenv pattern so pasted code refuses to boot.
title: Published valid-length HS256 signing keys in example and docs enable token forgery on copy-paste deployments

description: examples/fullstack/main.go builds the passkey ceremony-cookie HMAC key as `make([]byte, 32)` — 32 zero bytes, which passes the MinCookieKeyLength (32) gate and is known to every repo reader (PoC proves NewService accepts it). docs/content/docs/sdk/mfa.md publishes `[]byte("very-secure-32-byte-secret-key!!")` (exactly 32 bytes, passes the gate). A deployment copying either value HMACs ceremony cookies with an attacker-known key, letting the attacker forge ceremony-cookie state (challenge binding) that the server trusts. PoC proves both keys are accepted by passkey.NewService. Mitigating context: the example carries a 'replace with crypto/rand in production' comment and the failure mode requires copy-paste deployment; the ceremony still requires a real WebAuthn ceremony, bounding impact to ceremony-state forgery rather than direct authentication.
remediation: Replace the zero-key line with a crypto/rand generation snippet and a fail-fast guard (reject all-zero keys at NewService construction, e.g. compare against zero buffer); replace the docs literal with a generation snippet plus secret-manager guidance. Add the published docs string to a denylist so pasted deployments fail closed.
